headings: Many moralists invoke the “ self-evident ” nature of morality to substantiate their diverse notions of morality. Rigorously critique the intrinsic weaknesses in this argument.
Produce an extended essay for your argument Subjectivity of Self-Evidence .
Produce an extended essay for your argument Circular Reasoning .
Produce an extended essay for your argument Disagreement in Moral Intuitions .
Produce an extended essay for your argument Inapplicability of Mathematical Objectivity .
Produce an extended essay for your argument Contradictory Self-Evident Claims .
Produce a hypothetical dialogue between a moralist who invokes the “self-evident” nature of their own moral system and a moral non-realist.
Rebut the assumptions in Quiz Item #12 from the perspective of a moral non-realist.
Provide 20 discussion questions relevant to the content above.
intro: A sustained critique of appeals to moral self-evidence, preserving the original prompts, six analyses, dialogue, quiz and non-realist rejoinder. The revision distinguishes a feeling of certainty from justified self-evidence and repairs overclaims in the original formal arguments.
description: Original challenges to self-evident morality, with corrected logical scope and a careful distinction between validity and support for premises.
highlights: Disagreement challenges claims of reliable access; it does not by itself disprove moral truth.
Circular support and valid deduction are different issues.
The non-realist rejoinder remains distinct from the dialogue’s compromise.

replacements.1.1.0: Calling a moral claim self-evident does not settle its truth. The strongest critique asks how alleged direct justification can be distinguished from conditioning, error and prejudice. It should not assume that self-evidence means universal actual agreement. The arguments below retain the original structure while marking premises and inferences that require correction.
replacements.1.1.4: Premise 1 (disputed): if a proposition is self-evident, everyone recognizes it as true. This is stronger than the claim that adequate understanding can justify belief without inference.
replacements.1.1.5: Premise 2: at least some moral propositions lack universal recognition.
replacements.1.1.6: Conditional conclusion: if the disputed first premise holds, at least some moral propositions are not self-evident. The existential premise does not establish that none are.
replacements.1.1.17: A claim of direct, non-inferential justification is not automatically circular. Circularity arises when the only support for self-evidence is the proposition’s assumed truth and the only support for its truth is that alleged self-evidence.
replacements.1.1.29: These two biconditionals express the same equivalence; they are not tautologies. Without an independently warranted assertion of either side, they establish neither truth nor self-evidence.
replacements.1.1.31: Disagreement challenges an unqualified claim of effortless recognition. A defender must explain which disagreements reflect inadequate understanding without simply defining all dissenters as defective.
replacements.1.1.33: Premise 1 (disputed): every rational agent knows every self-evident proposition. Rationality alone does not guarantee attention, comprehension or freedom from error.
replacements.1.1.35: Conditional conclusion: the specified proposition is not self-evident if that strong recognition premise is accepted. This is not a proof about every moral proposition.
replacements.1.1.47: Mathematics provides useful comparisons, but an analogy cannot establish a moral claim’s objectivity. Proof from axioms, self-evidence of premises and mind-independent truth are separate questions.
replacements.1.1.49: Original premise to reject: mathematical truths are self-evident because they are provable. A difficult theorem can be proved without being self-evident; not every truth is provable in a specified formal system.
replacements.1.1.50: More defensible observation: competing moral systems often dispute their starting premises. Valid deductions from moral premises remain possible.
replacements.1.1.51: Repaired conclusion: a comparison with mathematics needs an account of why the proposed moral premises are justified. Absence of an agreed proof does not entail absence of self-evidence.
replacements.1.1.58: The original formulas below are retained as a failed argument to diagnose: neither premise supplies the needed implication S(p) → P(p).
replacements.1.1.61: The proposed conclusion ∀p(M(p) → ¬S(p)) does not follow. A counterexample sets T(p) false, M(p) true, P(p) false and S(p) true: both displayed premises hold while this conclusion fails.
replacements.1.1.65: Premise 1: p says action A is obligatory in specified circumstances and is claimed to be self-evident.
replacements.1.1.66: Premise 2: q denies that same obligation in the same circumstances and is also claimed to be self-evident.
replacements.1.1.78: If self-evidence entails truth, the two contradictory propositions cannot both be self-evident. It follows that at least one claim of self-evidence is mistaken, not that all such claims are.
replacements.1.1.80: An unsupported appeal to self-evidence is a weak public justification when competent disagreement persists. The critic can demand an account of comprehension, reliability and error correction. That challenge preserves the skeptical force of the original without treating disagreement, lack of proof or conflicting assertions as a demonstration that no moral truth exists.
replacements.2.1.2: This essay examines variation in what people experience as obvious. Its target is the unsupported transition from felt certainty to warranted moral belief. The formal arguments are conditional challenges to strong recognition claims; they do not establish moral non-realism merely from disagreement.
replacements.2.1.4: Self-evidence is commonly understood as justification available through adequate understanding rather than inference from other propositions. It need not mean immediate recognition by everybody. Axioms can also be adopted as starting assumptions without being self-evident. See Intuitionism in Ethics for the philosophical distinction.
replacements.2.1.5: Differences in upbringing, experience and social learning can affect apparent obviousness. These influences raise a reliability question, but a belief’s causal history alone does not determine its truth.
replacements.2.1.8: Premise 1 (a strong, contested interpretation): self-evidence entails universal actual recognition.
replacements.2.1.9: Premise 2: some moral propositions are not universally recognized.
replacements.2.1.10: Conditional conclusion: at least some moral propositions fail that strong interpretation of self-evidence.
replacements.2.1.11: This argument is valid only with a matched quantifier and the stated recognition premise. The premise is precisely what a defender of a more qualified account can reject.
replacements.2.1.18: This universal recognition condition is an assumption for the conditional argument, not an agreed definition.
replacements.2.1.22: Under that assumption, there exists at least one moral proposition that is not self-evident.
replacements.2.1.23: The existential conclusion concerns some propositions, not all. To challenge a particular claim, identify disagreement about that same proposition and defend the relevance of the dissenters’ understanding.
replacements.2.1.26: Hypothetical example: people may disagree about a family’s role in choosing a spouse. Distinguish consensual arranged marriage from forced marriage; disagreement about different practices is not disagreement about one identical proposition.
replacements.2.1.28: Example: people may differ about whether capital punishment is justified. Whether it deters crime is an empirical question, distinct from the moral judgment about punishment; neither is settled by calling it obvious.
replacements.2.1.30: Mathematical axioms are explicit starting points within specified systems. Alternative geometries illustrate why universal acceptance should not define their status. The moral analogy therefore needs more than a claim that mathematics is culturally uniform.
replacements.2.1.32: Axioms are adopted premises; some seem evident, while others are justified by their role in a theory.
replacements.2.1.33: A proof’s validity within a stated system differs from how people acquire, understand or accept that system.
replacements.2.1.36: Apparent self-evidence may reflect conditioning. Establishing that a particular belief is unreliable requires an argument, not merely the observation that it has social influences.
replacements.2.1.38: Persistent informed disagreement can weaken confidence in easy access to moral truth. It does not entail that every disputed proposition lacks direct justification.
replacements.2.1.44: This assumes rationality alone guarantees recognition; a more qualified account would require adequate understanding and relevant conditions.
replacements.2.1.46: The formula assumes one agent knows p and another does not. Observed disagreement alone does not establish which participant has knowledge, since knowledge entails truth.
replacements.2.1.50: The conclusion follows only under the strong recognition assumption for this specified p.
replacements.2.1.51: The structure is a conditional test, not an unconditional refutation of moral self-evidence.
replacements.2.1.53: Where an appeal fails to persuade, participants can make their assumptions and reasons available for criticism. This involves:
replacements.2.1.59: Variation in perceived obviousness supplies a serious challenge to unqualified appeals to self-evidence. The challenge concerns access and justification; it does not by itself decide whether objective moral truths exist. A successful defense must explain error and disagreement without assuming the very claim in dispute.
replacements.3.1.2: This essay targets a specific circular defense: p is true because self-evident, while its self-evidence is defended only by assuming p true. It distinguishes that failure of support from the separate proposal that some beliefs are justified without inference.
replacements.3.1.4: Begging the question occurs when the disputed conclusion supplies its own essential support. Such an argument can be deductively valid—p therefore p is valid—while providing no new reason for someone who doubts p.
replacements.3.1.9: An appeal becomes circular when the speaker defends it in the following way:
replacements.3.1.14: The exchange fails to provide independent support; its defect is explanatory and justificatory, not necessarily invalid deduction.
replacements.3.1.18: Conclusion: p is true. This is a valid inference from the two premises; the issue is whether the first premise has adequate support.
replacements.3.1.19: If the only defense of the first premise assumes p true, support is circular. A non-inferential account must instead explain the claimed direct warrant.
replacements.3.1.27: The reverse conditional is an additional claim, not something that follows from the first. Many true propositions are not self-evident.
replacements.3.1.30: The equivalence alone establishes neither side. Circular support arises only when each side is used as the sole warrant for the other; a biconditional is not inherently a fallacy.
replacements.3.1.32: A circular defense offers no new support to someone who doubts its premise. Merely asserting self-evidence can also be unsupported without literally being an argument in a circle.
replacements.3.1.41: To persuade a critic, offer reasons whose warrant does not depend solely on assuming the disputed conclusion. Possible resources include:
replacements.3.1.44: Ethical theories: expose their starting commitments and test consistency; being established does not itself make a theory true.
replacements.3.1.60: This proposed reverse implication needs justification; truth does not generally entail self-evidence.
replacements.3.1.64: The proposed defenses depend on each other. Truth itself does not become dependent on a person’s recognition of it.
replacements.3.1.65: The problem is lack of independent support, not failure of deductive validity. Validity asks whether true premises could yield a false conclusion.
replacements.3.1.71: Synthetic statements are not true solely by meaning. Whether all require empirical verification is disputed; the category of synthetic a priori judgment is central to this debate.
replacements.3.1.72: Many substantive moral claims are treated as synthetic, though accounts of moral language differ.
replacements.3.1.73: Calling a claim self-evident does not necessarily treat it as analytic: a defender may claim synthetic, non-inferential knowledge.
replacements.3.1.74: Thus the analytic/synthetic distinction does not prove circularity. The critic must examine the actual chain of support.
replacements.3.1.76: A sound argument is valid and has true premises. Agreement among participants is a separate matter affecting persuasion and shared inquiry.
replacements.3.1.80: Unsupported attribution of self-evidence can leave a critic without a reason to accept a premise. It is not automatically equivalent to assuming a conclusion within an argument.
replacements.3.1.83: A mathematical analogy cannot settle which moral claims have direct warrant; neither field requires universal actual agreement for truth.
replacements.3.1.84: People can differ in what seems obvious. Whether any seeming provides justification remains the question, rather than an established premise that morality is subjective.
replacements.3.1.87: An intuition may be challenged as unreliable or unsupported. It is circular only if its defense relies on the claim it is supposed to justify.
replacements.3.1.94: The circular version of an appeal to self-evidence fails to give a doubter independent support. A stronger critique distinguishes that failure from deductive invalidity and from non-inferential justification. It asks defenders how direct warrant is recognized, how error is detected and why dissent should reduce or preserve confidence.
replacements.3.1.99: Kant, Immanuel. Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals. A primary work on rational foundations of ethics; it should not be summarized as simply rejecting all self-evidence.
replacements.3.1.100: Reference correction: the original attribution “James Van Cleve, Foundations of Logic and Mathematics” could not be substantiated and should not be treated as a verified book citation. For the issue discussed here, consult the linked Stanford Encyclopedia entry on ethical intuitionism.
replacements.4.1.2: Persistent disagreement challenges claims that moral truth is readily available through reflection. This essay examines the strength and limits of that challenge, without inferring non-realism solely from the existence of dissent.
replacements.4.1.12: The following argument depends on a strong recognition assumption. Rationality alone may not ensure adequate understanding of a particular proposition.
replacements.4.1.13: Premise 1 (contested): every rational agent recognizes every self-evident moral truth.
replacements.4.1.14: Premise 2: rational agents disagree about at least some specified moral propositions.
replacements.4.1.15: Conditional conclusion: those disputed propositions fail this strong recognition condition; the argument does not cover every moral proposition.
replacements.4.1.16: A defender can dispute the recognition premise. The critic should then ask for independently identifiable conditions of adequate understanding.
replacements.4.1.24: The formula states the strong recognition assumption being tested, rather than an agreed definition of self-evidence.
replacements.4.1.26: The formula assumes one participant knows p and another does not. Mere disagreement supplies conflicting beliefs, not knowledge of which belief is true.
replacements.4.1.32: For this p, the conclusion is conditional on the recognition premise and the stronger knowledge assumption.
replacements.4.1.33: This identifies the burden of defending recognition conditions; it does not refute all direct moral justification.
replacements.4.1.35: Some accounts connect self-evidence to adequate understanding. The critic can press whether persistent informed disagreement remains after relevant facts, meanings and circumstances have been aligned.
replacements.4.1.36: Conditional challenge: if adequate understanding guarantees recognition, disagreement among people meeting that condition threatens the claim.
replacements.4.1.38: Variation can support concern about reliability, but it does not logically establish that there is no objective answer.
replacements.4.1.40: Relativism is one possible explanation, not a consequence of disagreement. A realist can instead attribute error to one or more participants.
replacements.4.1.42: Moral relativism makes moral truth relative to a standard, culture or perspective. Disagreement alone does not establish that theory, just as scientific disagreement does not establish relative scientific truth.
replacements.4.1.43: Tolerance is a possible additional commitment; it does not follow from relativism, which could also describe an intolerant local standard.
replacements.4.1.46: Constructivism grounds principles in a specified procedure of practical reasoning; it need not identify truth with whatever a society happens to agree on.
replacements.4.1.48: Participants can seek publicly assessable reasons beyond the bare assertion of self-evidence. This practical recommendation does not assume that all justification must be inferential.
replacements.4.1.52: Utilitarianism: typically assesses consequences by aggregate welfare; “greatest number” alone can conceal intensity and distribution.
replacements.4.1.56: Informed disagreement weakens a bare assertion that everyone who thinks properly must agree. It calls for an account of understanding, error and reliability. The result is a challenge to justification, not a demonstration of relativism or the nonexistence of moral truth.
replacements.5.1.2: The analogy with mathematical objectivity deserves scrutiny: it does not independently establish any moral premise. The critique below distinguishes objectivity from proof and self-evidence, correcting the original attempt to infer non-self-evidence from the absence of agreed moral axioms.
replacements.5.1.4: A mathematical proof establishes a conclusion from stated axioms under specified inference rules. Whether mathematical objects or truths are mind-independent is a further philosophical question.
replacements.5.1.5: Axiomatic foundations: starting assumptions of a system, not necessarily truths obvious to everyone.
replacements.5.1.7: Checkable derivation: competent readers can inspect a proof within a stated system; universal actual acceptance is not required.
replacements.5.1.9: Pythagorean theorem: a²+b²=c² for a right triangle in Euclidean geometry. The geometric setting matters.
replacements.5.1.11: Mathematics uses varied systems, while moral inquiry often disputes foundational commitments and application. Calling all morality a human construct would already assume one answer to the metaethical question.
replacements.5.1.14: Disputed premises: moral arguments can be deductively valid, even when their premises lack agreement.
replacements.5.1.15: Context: moral applications depend on facts about agents and situations; this alone does not establish that all moral principles are contingent.
replacements.5.1.20: No single agreed foundation: disagreement over basic commitments complicates moral proof, but mathematics also has alternative axiomatic systems.
replacements.5.1.26: Original premise to reject: provability makes every mathematical truth self-evident. Proof and self-evidence are different forms of justification.
replacements.5.1.27: Observation: moral reasoning often lacks agreed starting premises. This is not the universal claim that no moral proposition is logically provable.
replacements.5.1.28: Repaired conclusion: the mathematical analogy does not itself justify moral axioms or show that they are self-evident.
replacements.5.1.34: The original formulas are retained below as an invalid proposed argument, with their defects identified:
replacements.5.1.36: The displayed universal claim is too strong: mathematical truth does not entail both provability in a specified system and self-evidence.
replacements.5.1.38: The displayed universal denial of moral proof is unsupported. One can validly derive moral conclusions from normative premises.
replacements.5.1.40: The proposed inference from lack of proof to lack of self-evidence is invalid without the additional premise S(p) → P(p), which would itself need defense.
replacements.5.1.41: This conclusion does not follow. Let M be true, P false, S true and T false for one p; the original two premises are satisfied while the conclusion is false.
replacements.5.1.42: The logical exercise therefore exposes a flaw in the original critique. The defensible objection concerns an unsupported analogy, not a proof that all moral self-evidence is impossible.
replacements.5.1.44: The comparison leaves moral objectivity unresolved. A lack of consensus or proof does not determine what is true independently of belief.
replacements.5.1.45: Justification: disputed axioms require explanation; their disputed status does not itself establish subjectivism.
replacements.5.1.46: Diversity: varying moral codes prompt questions about reliability and error, without entailing relativism.
replacements.5.1.48: Constructivism: principles may be justified through an idealized procedure of reasoning rather than mere collective agreement.
replacements.5.1.51: Reply: an intuitive starting point needs an account of reliability and correction. Universal agreement is neither supplied nor sufficient to establish truth.
replacements.5.1.53: Reply: broad agreement may be evidence about shared intuitions, but it is not by itself proof of objective truth or universal binding force. Disagreement also does not prove the opposite.
replacements.5.1.55: Mathematical objectivity is an analogy to investigate, not a shortcut to moral justification. The original argument confused proof with self-evidence and drew an invalid conclusion. A stronger skeptical challenge asks what warrants the proposed moral starting points and how inquiry could identify error.
replacements.6.1.6: Recognition: adequate understanding is proposed as a condition of access; universal actual assent is a stronger claim.
replacements.6.1.7: Justification: apparent obviousness is not a guarantee that a person’s attribution of self-evidence is correct.
replacements.6.1.20: Premise 1: p says A is obligatory in specified circumstances and is asserted to be self-evident.
replacements.6.1.21: Premise 2: q denies the same obligation under those same circumstances and is also asserted to be self-evident.
replacements.6.1.31: If self-evidence entails truth, genuine self-evidence of both would yield O(A) and ¬O(A). Merely reporting that two people claim it does not itself assert a contradiction as true.
replacements.6.1.33: At least one attribution must be mistaken. This demonstrates fallibility of attribution, not that no proposition could be self-evident.
replacements.6.1.35: Conflicting attributions show that a feeling of certainty cannot certify every claim. Universal truth, where it exists, is compatible with people making mistakes about it.
replacements.6.1.36: Apparent obviousness varies; the status of genuine self-evidence remains the disputed issue.
replacements.6.1.39: Resolution: the bare label offers no shared way to choose between claims. A defender may propose criteria, whose adequacy then needs examination.
replacements.6.1.44: These claims conflict only where they apply to the same speech and circumstances. A qualified right can coexist with specified restrictions.
replacements.6.1.47: Such principles can pull in different directions in cases involving vaccination or conscription. A conflict of defeasible reasons is not automatically a formal contradiction.
replacements.6.1.57: Relativism interprets moral truth relative to a standard; it is one account of variation, not a conclusion forced by it.
replacements.6.1.61: Constructivism proposes justification through a specified practical procedure; it is broader than actual social agreement.
replacements.6.1.66: Utilitarianism evaluates consequences in terms of aggregate welfare, with variants concerning rules and acts.
replacements.6.1.71: Contradictory claims cannot both be true in the same sense and circumstances. Their competing claims to self-evidence show that attribution is fallible and a bare appeal cannot settle the dispute. That limited conclusion motivates scrutiny without establishing that both claims are false or that moral truth is impossible.
replacements.7.1.6: NR: That could become circular if “proper reflection” means only arriving at your conclusion. Can you specify what counts as adequate understanding independently of whether someone agrees?
replacements.7.1.8: NR: Axioms are not always self-evident, and a proof from axioms is different from direct justification. Your comparison still leaves the warrant for a proposed moral axiom unexplained.
replacements.7.1.10: NR: I am skeptical of objective moral truth, but this analogy alone proves neither side. Lack of an agreed moral proof does not logically establish non-objectivity.
replacements.7.1.14: NR: Suppose p says A is obligatory and q denies that same obligation in identical circumstances. Both cannot be true. People may nevertheless describe each as obvious, as in disputes over the permissibility of a specific assisted-death case.
replacements.7.1.18: NR: Then identify those conditions without defining every dissenter as irrational. Persistent informed disagreement makes that a substantial burden, even if it is not a conclusive disproof.
replacements.7.1.20: NR: Bias and misunderstanding may explain some disagreement, but that explanation needs evidence in each case. Otherwise it protects a favored view from every possible criticism.
replacements.7.1.22: NR: As a non-realist, I would not describe our aim as discovering stance-independent moral facts. We can still examine consistency, consequences and shared aims, and use ethical theories to clarify commitments.
replacements.7.1.24: NR: Agreed. Those theories can organize discussion without certifying objective morality. Defenders of direct justification can also be open to criticism; the practical distinction is whether a view permits its claims to be questioned.
replacements.7.1.35: What feels self-evident can be shaped by intuition and social learning; that differs from establishing whether direct justification exists.
replacements.7.1.41: Persistent informed disagreement challenges an unqualified recognition claim without disproving every form of self-evidence.
replacements.7.1.44: The analogy requires an explanation of the proposed moral premises; proof and self-evidence must be distinguished.
replacements.7.1.45: Mathematical derivation works within stated systems; axioms and moral premises need not enjoy universal actual acceptance.
replacements.7.1.48: The bare label supplies no agreed resolution; additional criteria are needed to assess the competing attributions.
replacements.9.1.0: From a moral non-realist perspective, Quiz Item #12 risks implying that better reasoning must uncover objective moral facts. That implication is not required by the question itself. The rejoinder below challenges a realist reading while retaining the practical value of clearer, more consistent deliberation.
replacements.9.1.2: A non-realist who denies stance-independent moral facts will not regard discussion as a route to discovering such facts. Discussion may still clarify preferences, reduce factual error, reveal inconsistency and coordinate action. These achievements should not be confused with demonstrating moral realism.
replacements.9.1.4: Non-realism includes different positions. Noncognitivists analyze moral utterances as expressing attitudes or commitments; error theorists treat ordinary moral claims as truth-apt but systematically mistaken. Logic can test consequences and consistency within either debate; logic alone does not supply a disputed normative starting point.
replacements.9.1.8: Deontology starts from duties or rights. A non-realist can ask what supports their stance-independent authority without assuming that no reason of any kind can favor them.
replacements.9.1.10: On this non-realist interpretation, the frameworks articulate and organize commitments. Their practical usefulness does not by itself establish stance-independent moral facts, and disagreement among them alone does not disprove those facts.
replacements.9.1.12: The strongest rejoinder rejects the slide from improving deliberation to discovering objective moral truth. Non-realists can value consistency, accurate information and negotiation in relation to their aims. Quiz Item #12 need not assume realism unless “improvement” is defined as closer access to stance-independent moral facts.

bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer0: Apparent certainty alone does not establish that a moral claim has direct justification or is true.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer1: By challenging reliability, disagreement and unsupported appeals; disagreement alone does not prove non-realism.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer2: Circular support assumes the disputed claim in its own defense. Direct, non-inferential justification is a different proposal.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer3: The circular version says p is true because self-evident and self-evident solely because p is true. Requiring reflection is not itself that circle.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer4: The analogy does not supply a reason to accept a particular moral starting point; mathematical proof and self-evidence differ.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer5: Mathematical proofs use stated axioms and rules. Neither universal actual agreement nor self-evidence of every mathematical truth is required.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer6: At least one attribution of self-evidence must be mistaken when the propositions are strict contradictories in identical circumstances.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer7: Whether the same assisted-death act is permissible under the same specified circumstances; differing circumstances or qualified principles may dissolve an apparent contradiction.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer8: Criteria and reasons whose warrant does not depend solely on the disputed conclusion, while recognizing the limits of what this establishes.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer9: Proof from premises differs from self-evidence of a premise. Lack of agreed moral proof does not imply lack of all direct justification.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer10: By asking what warrants the proposed intuitions and how error can be identified, rather than demanding universal actual agreement.
bareAnswerReplacements.8.1.answer11: Use dialogue, logical consistency and evidence about consequences to clarify and revise commitments. These practices need not assume that objective moral facts exist.
